newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban report victory north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban report victory north of Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's radical Islamic Taleban militia said on Sunday it had driven opposition forces out of two districts in an overnight attack north of the Afghan capital Kabul.

Taleban-controlled Kabul radio said that Taleban forces had cleared Mir Bachakot and Guldara districts of forces loyal to ousted government commander Ahmad Shah Masood and northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.
The Sunday night broadcast, monitored in Islamabad, said the northwards advance against "evil forces" was continuing.
There was no independent confirmation of the report.

The Kabul broadcast said the deputy chief of the Taleban ruling council in the capital, Mullah Mohammad Hasan Akhund, visited frontlines and quoted him as saying in Mir Bacha Kot that Taleban forces were fighting with a high morale.

Earlier on Sunday, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, AIP, quoted Taleban sources as saying the Islamic militia had launched a successful attack on the northern alliance forces on a front that has been at stalemate for several weeks.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted the sources as saying in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar, where the purist Islamic Taleban has its headquarters, as saying that at least 24 fighters from both sides were killed or wounded.
The agency quoted the sources as saying Taleban fighters had entered the village of Kalakan, 25 km (19 miles) north of Kabul that had been occupied by Masood's forces.
The Taleban captured Kabul on September 27 and then pushed north before being rolled back by a Masood counter-offensive. Masood was then joined by Dostum.
For the past few weeks, the two sides have been fighting over a band of hills that runs part way across the Shamali valley around Kalakan.
Attempts by the United Nations and Pakistan to forge a ceasefire that would lead to peace talks to end 17 years of civil war in Afghanistan have so far come to nothing.
Taleban officials in Kabul said earlier Saturday's attack was launched along the so-called old road which runs up the western side of the broad valley that runs north from Kabul.
Throughout Saturday night and Sunday morning, the sound of rocket and artillery fire was clearly audible in Kabul itself, some 20 km (13 miles) from the scene of the fighting.
Both sides were still exchanging heavy barrages of artillery and rockets on Sunday morning.

Taleban multi-barrelled rocket launchers were firing salvo after salvo of rockets towards the positions of the alliance forces while behind the front lines, tank crews were cleaning shells in preparation for going up to the lines.
A steady trickle of families -- their possessions loaded on to donkeys and wheelbarrows -- moved south.
A shepherd who was also moving south with his livestock told Reuters in Kabul: "This is the heaviest fighting I have seen since the Taleban were forced back (in mid-October)."
On the Kabul front, the Taleban hold a strategic line of low hills that the alliance must capture if they are to launch an offensive against Kabul itself.
The Taleban have vowed to disarm other armed groups in Afghanistan and impose their puritanical vision of Islam on the whole country.
The Taleban have agreed in principle to the necessity of a ceasefire, but their demands are unlikely to be acceptable to their opposition.
